analysis.one_liner: Funds nationwide testing and enforcement to catch housing and mortgage discrimination.
analysis.headline: The Housing Fairness Act of 2025, introduced with a single cosponsor, has sat without action in the House Financial Services Committee since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct HUD to run a nationwide program that sends matched pairs of testers — for example, one white and one Black applicant with identical finances — to landlords, home sellers, and mortgage lenders to document differences in treatment based on race, religion, sex, familial status, disability, or national origin. It would raise annual funding for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program to $42.5 million, mostly for nonprofit groups that help discrimination victims, and add $20 million a year for the testing program and for grants to study and pilot solutions to housing segregation. Test results could be used as evidence in enforcement actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, homebuyers, and mortgage borrowers who face discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability, or national origin, plus the nonprofit fair housing organizations that represent them.

how_it_helps.text: HUD must run a nationwide testing program that detects and documents differences in how renters, homebuyers, and mortgage borrowers are treated, and measures how prevalent discriminatory practices are across housing and lending markets [S3].
Testing results could be used as the basis for federal, state, or local enforcement actions to remedy discriminatory housing practices, giving victims and enforcers harder evidence [S3].

The bill reauthorizes the Fair Housing Initiatives Program through FY2028 at $42.5 million a year, with at least 75 percent going to private enforcement initiatives run by nonprofit organizations that assist discrimination victims [S3].

It adds a $5 million-a-year matching grant program for nonprofits to study the causes and effects of housing discrimination and segregation — including on veterans and military personnel — and run pilot projects testing solutions [S3].

It requires HUD to report biennially to Congress on testing outcomes and annually on hotline and website contacts, and directs the Secretary to maintain a national fair housing education and outreach program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund about $62.5 million a year in authorized spending; landlords, home sellers, and mortgage lenders bear the cost of heightened scrutiny and any enforcement actions that documented discrimination triggers.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $62.5 million a year in new federal spending through FY2028, and authorization is not the same as an appropriation — Congress would still have to fund it [S3].

Testing-based enforcement relies on paired comparisons that can be imperfect evidence, and the bill directs at least 75 percent of Fair Housing Initiatives Program funds to private enforcement rather than to directly helping families with housing costs [S3].
Grants require nonprofits to put up matching funds worth 50 percent of the award, which favors larger, established organizations over smaller ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted investment: about $62.5 million a year to document discrimination that already is illegal under the Fair Housing Act and to fund the nonprofits that help victims enforce their rights. The main cost is taxpayer money and the risk that paired testing occasionally misreads a landlord's or lender's conduct. It does nothing on its own to lower rents or mortgage costs, so its value depends entirely on how well HUD runs the testing program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced in January 2025 and has had no further action since, so it has never come up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Green introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
It has one cosponsor, a House Democrat, and no further committee or floor action has been taken in more than a year of the 119th Congress [S4,S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and mortgage lenders avoid the heightened testing and enforcement risk the bill would have created, and fair housing nonprofits do not receive the increased funding it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and lenders; fair housing nonprofits left unfunded

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; it has never been reported out or scheduled for a vote.

against.name: Chair French Hill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are House Democrats, no Republicans joined, and no floor vote has occurred.

industries.note: The bill would make these groups the funded channel for fair housing enforcement: $42.5 million a year for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, at least 75 percent for private enforcement initiatives, plus testing contracts and matching grants [S3]. Their interest runs with victims of discrimination, since the funding pays for assistance to people who have faced it.

Nationwide paired testing could document discriminatory treatment of renters, and the results may be used as the basis for enforcement actions, creating legal and financial risk for landlords who treat protected groups worse [S3].

The testing program extends to borrowers seeking home mortgage loans and refinancing, so lenders whose treatment of borrowers varies by race, national origin, or other protected traits would face documented evidence usable in enforcement [S3].

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, one cosponsor, and no committee action in over a year, the bill is very unlikely to advance. Bills at this stage typically die quietly at the end of the Congress unless the Financial Services Committee chooses to take it up, which would require new interest from its leadership.
